fields.Question: Design the database schema for a URL shortener that handles 100M new links a month and is read-heavy (100:1). How do you generate the short code and what do you index?
fields.Answer:
Approach: one core table keyed by the short code, with the code generated so it never collides and never needs a lookup-before-insert.

CREATE TABLE links (
  id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,          -- from a sequence or ID service
  code        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,        -- base62(id) or random 7 chars
  target_url  TEXT NOT NULL,
  owner_id    BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX links_owner_created ON links (owner_id, created_at DESC);
  • Code generation: base62 of a unique integer id gives 7 chars for about 3.5 trillion ids and cannot collide; random codes hide volume but need a UNIQUE constraint and retry on conflict.
  • Reads are a single point lookup on code; put a cache (Redis or CDN) in front since links are immutable.
  • Click analytics go to a separate append-only events table or stream, never an UPDATE counter on the hot row.
  • Scale: shard or partition by hash of code; the lookup path never needs a cross-shard query.

Pitfalls: sequential base62 codes are guessable (enumeration), so mix with a bijective shuffle if privacy matters; incrementing a click counter on the link row creates a write hotspot.

Follow-ups: custom aliases (same UNIQUE column, check reserved words), expiry (partial index or TTL job), deduplicating the same long URL (optional unique hash of target per owner).
fields.Hint: Point lookup by code, immutable rows, cache everything, keep analytics off the hot row.
fields.Fact: Generate codes from a unique id so there is no collision check, and keep counters out of the read path.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: CREATE INDEX (CONCURRENTLY) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html)

fields.Question: Design tables for an e-commerce site: customers, products, orders and order line items. A product's price can change after an order is placed. What do you store where?
fields.Answer:
Key insight: an order is a historical record, so copy the price (and anything legally relevant like product name and tax) onto the line item at purchase time. Do not join back to the live product price.

CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INT NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled')),
  total_cents INT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id BIGINT REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id BIGINT REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price_cents INT NOT NULL,     -- snapshot at purchase
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
  • Money as integer cents (or NUMERIC), never FLOAT.
  • Status as a constrained column (CHECK or enum) plus an order_events table if you need the audit trail.
  • total_cents is denormalized for fast listing; compute it in the same transaction that writes the items.
  • Index foreign keys you filter on: customer order history is (customer_id, created_at DESC).

Pitfalls: float money, reading the current product price for old invoices, forgetting an index on order_items(product_id) if you ever delete products or query sales by product.

Follow-ups: inventory reservation under concurrency, multi-currency (store currency per order), soft-deleting products that old orders reference.
fields.Hint: Orders are history: snapshot prices onto the line item.
fields.Fact: Line items copy the unit price at purchase time so later price changes never rewrite old orders.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

fields.Question: Design the schema for a Twitter-like app: users, follows and posts, plus the home timeline. Users follow up to thousands of accounts, and a few accounts have millions of followers.
fields.Answer:
Core tables:

CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  followee_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
CREATE INDEX follows_followee ON follows (followee_id, follower_id);
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,           -- time-ordered id (Snowflake style)
  author_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  body TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX posts_author_id ON posts (author_id, id DESC);

Timeline: two strategies.

  • Fan-out on read: query posts WHERE author_id IN (followees) ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 50. Cheap writes, expensive reads with many followees.
  • Fan-out on write: on each post, push the post id into every follower's timeline list (Redis or a timelines table). Cheap reads, but a celebrity post means millions of writes.
  • Hybrid (what Twitter described): fan-out on write for normal users, merge celebrity posts in at read time.

Why two indexes on follows: the PK serves who-do-I-follow, the reverse index serves who-follows-me (needed for fan-out and follower counts).

Pitfalls: COUNT(*) of followers on every profile view (keep a counter table updated asynchronously); offset pagination on the timeline (use keyset on id).

Follow-ups: unfollow cleanup in materialized timelines, privacy (blocked users filtered at read).
fields.Hint: Fan-out on write vs read, hybrid for celebrities.
fields.Fact: Home timelines trade write amplification against read cost; the hybrid handles high-follower accounts.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Design a booking table for a hotel or meeting-room system so that the database itself guarantees no two bookings of the same room overlap in time, even under concurrent requests.
fields.Answer:
Key insight: an application check (SELECT then INSERT) races under concurrency. Push the invariant into the database.

PostgreSQL: exclusion constraint on a range.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  during TSTZRANGE NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
-- [start, end) half-open ranges, so back-to-back bookings do not conflict
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, during)
VALUES (42, tstzrange('2026-05-01 10:00', '2026-05-01 11:00', '[)'));

A concurrent overlapping insert fails with an exclusion violation, which the app maps to 'room taken'.

  • Without exclusion constraints (MySQL): model time as discrete slots (room_id, night) with a UNIQUE key, or lock the room row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before checking, or use SERIALIZABLE.
  • Hotels are usually per-night inventory, so a (room_type_id, date) counter row decremented with a guarded UPDATE also works: UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE ... AND available > 0.

Pitfalls: closed intervals making 10:00-11:00 and 11:00-12:00 conflict; check-then-insert under READ COMMITTED (classic write skew).

Follow-ups: holds that expire (status plus expires_at, cleanup job), cancellations (exclude only active rows with a WHERE clause on the constraint).
fields.Hint: Let the database enforce non-overlap: exclusion constraint or slot rows with UNIQUE.
fields.Fact: Check-then-insert races; constraints or row locks make double booking impossible.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You are building a B2B SaaS app with 5,000 customer companies of very different sizes. How do you model multi-tenancy in the database? Compare the options.
fields.Answer:
• Shared tables with tenant_id on every row: cheapest, easiest migrations, scales to many small tenants. Risk: one missing WHERE leaks data. Mitigate with row-level security and composite keys starting with tenant_id.
  • Schema per tenant: better isolation and per-tenant restore, but thousands of schemas make migrations slow and strain catalog and connection pooling.
  • Database per tenant: strongest isolation, per-tenant scaling and compliance, highest ops cost. Usually reserved for a few large or regulated customers.

Typical answer: shared tables with tenant_id for the long tail, plus the ability to move a whale tenant to its own database or shard. tenant_id becomes the shard key, so every query is single-shard.

CREATE TABLE projects (
  tenant_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
);
ALTER TABLE projects ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON projects
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);

Pitfalls: indexes that do not lead with tenant_id (cross-tenant scans), noisy neighbours, unique constraints that forget tenant_id (UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) not UNIQUE (email)).

Follow-ups: per-tenant backups and deletion (GDPR), connection pooling with RLS (set the setting per transaction).
fields.Hint: tenant_id everywhere, leading every key; isolate whales.
fields.Fact: Shared schema with tenant_id plus row-level security is the default; move large tenants out when needed.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Row Security Policies (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)
Vitess Documentation: Sharding (https://vitess.io/docs/reference/features/sharding/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Design storage for a chat app (like Slack or WhatsApp): conversations, members, messages and per-user unread counts. The hot query is 'last 50 messages in a conversation' and 'which conversations have unread messages for me'.
fields.Answer:
CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  seq BIGINT NOT NULL,              -- per-conversation increasing number
  sender_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  body TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, seq)
);
CREATE TABLE memberships (
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  conversation_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  last_read_seq BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, conversation_id)
);
  • Last 50: WHERE conversation_id = $1 ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 50, served directly by the PK. Older pages use seq < $last_seen (keyset).
  • Unread: store a read cursor (last_read_seq) per membership instead of a row per user per message. Unread count = conversation's latest seq minus last_read_seq.
  • Keep last_seq on the conversation row (or compute MAX(seq) from the PK) for that comparison.
  • At large scale this maps naturally to a wide-column store (Cassandra: partition key conversation_id, clustering key seq), with bucketing by time so partitions stay bounded.

Pitfalls: a read-receipt row per message per user (N times M writes), global auto-increment ids as the ordering key across shards, unbounded partitions for huge channels.

Follow-ups: generating seq without contention (counter per conversation updated in the same transaction, or a per-partition sequence), edits and deletes (tombstones), search (separate index).
fields.Hint: Read cursor per member, not read flags per message.
fields.Fact: Per-conversation sequence numbers give cheap pagination and unread counts via a single cursor.
fields.Source:
Apache Cassandra Documentation: Data Modeling (https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/data-modeling/index.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Blog posts can have many tags and tags apply to many posts. Design it and write the query for 'posts that have ALL of the tags python and postgres'.
fields.Answer:
CREATE TABLE tags (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE post_tags (
  post_id BIGINT REFERENCES posts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id  BIGINT REFERENCES tags(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id)
);
CREATE INDEX post_tags_tag ON post_tags (tag_id, post_id);

-- relational division: posts having all requested tags
SELECT pt.post_id
FROM post_tags pt
JOIN tags t ON t.id = pt.tag_id
WHERE t.name IN ('python', 'postgres')
GROUP BY pt.post_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT t.id) = 2;
  • ANY of the tags: drop the HAVING (and add DISTINCT).
  • The composite PK serves 'tags of a post'; the reverse index serves 'posts with a tag'.
  • Alternative: a tags TEXT[] column with a GIN index and tags @> ARRAY['python','postgres']. Simpler reads, but no referential integrity and renaming a tag means rewriting rows.

Pitfalls: comma-separated tag strings (cannot index or join), forgetting the reverse index, COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT) when duplicates are possible.

Follow-ups: tag counts for a tag cloud (cached counter), case-insensitive tag names (unique index on lower(name)).
fields.Hint: Junction table; ALL-of is GROUP BY plus HAVING COUNT = n.
fields.Fact: Matching all of a set is relational division: filter, group, and require the count to equal the set size.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: JSON Types (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)

fields.Question: Design storage for threaded comments (Reddit style) of arbitrary depth. You need to fetch a whole thread and a subtree efficiently. What are the options?
fields.Answer:
• Adjacency list (parent_id): simplest, cheap inserts and moves. Fetch a subtree with a recursive CTE.
  • Materialized path (path = '1/7/42/'): subtree is path LIKE '1/7/%' with a btree index (text_pattern_ops in Postgres) or the ltree extension. Moving a subtree rewrites all descendants' paths.
  • Closure table (ancestor, descendant, depth): any subtree or ancestor query is a single indexed join; costs O(depth) rows per node.
  • Nested sets: fast reads, very expensive inserts. Rarely the right answer for a write-heavy comment system.
WITH RECURSIVE thread AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, body, 1 AS depth
  FROM comments WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.body, t.depth + 1
  FROM comments c JOIN thread t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM thread;

Practical answer: adjacency list plus post_id on every comment. Fetching a whole post's thread is WHERE post_id = $1 (indexed) and you build the tree in application code in O(n). Recursive CTE only for true subtrees.

Pitfalls: recursion without an index on parent_id, cycles if moves are allowed (add a depth limit), loading huge threads at once (paginate top level and lazy-load deep branches).

Follow-ups: sort by score within each level, collapse deep threads.
fields.Hint: Adjacency list plus post_id; recursive CTE for subtrees; closure table if read-heavy.
fields.Fact: Store parent_id and the root post id, then assemble the tree in memory for the common case.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Product wants a full change history for the accounts table: who changed what and when, and the ability to see an account as of any past date. How do you design it?
fields.Answer:
• History table (type 2 style): account_versions(account_id, valid_from, valid_to, ...all columns..., changed_by). Current row has valid_to NULL or infinity. As-of query: WHERE account_id = $1 AND valid_from <= $t AND (valid_to > $t OR valid_to IS NULL).
  • Populate it in the same transaction as the change, either from the application or with a trigger, so history cannot diverge from the current state.
  • Audit log alternative: append-only account_events(account_id, at, actor, diff jsonb). Great for who-changed-what; reconstructing state as-of requires replaying.
  • CDC alternative: stream the WAL or binlog (Debezium) into a warehouse. No app changes, but history lives outside the OLTP database.
CREATE TABLE account_versions (
  account_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  valid_to   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  email TEXT, plan TEXT,
  changed_by BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (account_id, valid_from)
);

Pitfalls: writing history asynchronously (lost on crash), using app server clocks for ordering across servers, unbounded growth (partition history by time).

Follow-ups: GDPR erasure versus immutable history (crypto-shredding or redaction), SQL:2011 system-versioned tables in MariaDB, SQL Server and others.
fields.Hint: Versioned rows with valid_from/valid_to written in the same transaction.
fields.Fact: Write history in the same transaction as the change; choose versions for as-of queries and events for who-did-what.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

fields.Question: An interviewer shows a single wide table orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_email, customer_address, product_1, product_2, product_3, ...). What is wrong and how would you fix it? When would you deliberately denormalize?
fields.Answer:
Problems:

  • Repeating groups (product_1..3): fixed limit, cannot index or query 'orders containing product X' cleanly. Violates 1NF.
  • Customer data duplicated on every order: update anomalies (change email in one row, others stale), insert anomalies (no customer without an order), delete anomalies (delete last order loses the customer).

Fix: customers, orders (FK to customer), order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price), products. Each fact stored once (3NF).

Deliberate denormalization:

  • Historical snapshots: the shipping address and price at time of order belong on the order, because they must not change later. That is not duplication, it is a different fact.
  • Read-heavy aggregates: order total, comment counts, follower counts, kept in sync in the same transaction or asynchronously with reconciliation.
  • Analytics: star schemas in a warehouse are intentionally denormalized.

Pitfalls: denormalizing before measuring, keeping derived counts without a repair job.

Strong candidate line: normalize for correctness in OLTP, denormalize specific read paths with a clear owner for keeping them consistent.
fields.Hint: Spot update/insert/delete anomalies; normalize, then denormalize on purpose.
fields.Fact: Normalize so each fact lives once; denormalize only specific, measured read paths with a sync strategy.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: The team wants 'soft delete' on users (deleted_at column) instead of DELETE. What problems does this cause and how do you design around them?
fields.Answer:
• Every query must filter deleted_at IS NULL; one forgotten filter leaks deleted data. Use a view or ORM default scope, or row-level security.
  • Unique constraints break: a deleted user still holds the email. Use a partial unique index:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live
  ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
  • Foreign keys still point to soft-deleted rows; ON DELETE CASCADE no longer fires, so children need their own handling.
  • Index bloat: dead rows stay in every index; partial indexes on WHERE deleted_at IS NULL keep hot indexes small.
  • Legal deletion (GDPR): soft delete is not erasure; you still need a hard-delete or anonymize job.

Alternative: hard delete plus an archive table (move the row to users_archive in the same transaction). Main table stays clean, constraints work normally, recovery is a copy back.

Answer shape: soft delete is fine for user-facing undo windows, but scope it, use partial indexes, and purge after retention.
fields.Hint: Partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.
fields.Fact: Soft delete needs partial unique indexes and a default filter, or use an archive table instead.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Partial Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Row Security Policies (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)

fields.Question: Should the primary key of a high-insert table (say 50k inserts per second) be an auto-increment BIGINT, a random UUIDv4, or something else? Justify for both PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB.
fields.Answer:
• Auto-increment BIGINT: compact (8 bytes), inserts append to the right edge of the btree so pages stay hot and full. Downsides: guessable, needs a central sequence, awkward to merge across shards or generate offline.
  • Random UUIDv4: generated anywhere, no coordination, not guessable. But random inserts land all over the btree: page splits, poor cache locality, more WAL and write amplification. In InnoDB it is worse because the PK is the clustered index (the table itself is ordered by it) and every secondary index stores the PK, so a 16-byte random key bloats everything.
  • Time-ordered ids: UUIDv7, ULID, Snowflake: globally unique without coordination and roughly monotonic, so inserts stay near the right edge. This is usually the best answer for distributed systems.

Answer: BIGINT identity for a single-node app; UUIDv7 or Snowflake-style ids when ids are generated by many services or exposed publicly. Store UUIDs in a native uuid or BINARY(16) column, never as a 36-char string.

Pitfalls: exposing sequential ids in URLs (enumeration and leaking volume), UUIDs as VARCHAR(36), assuming UUIDv7 ordering is exact across machines (it is only roughly ordered by clock).

Follow-ups: using a BIGINT internal key plus a public random slug; sequence caching and gaps.
fields.Hint: Random keys scatter btree inserts; time-ordered ids keep locality.
fields.Fact: Random UUIDv4 keys hurt btree locality, especially with InnoDB clustering; prefer BIGINT or time-ordered UUIDv7.
fields.Source:
MySQL Reference Manual: Clustered and Secondary Indexes (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-index-types.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Given employees(id, name, salary), write a query returning the second highest distinct salary, or NULL if there is none. Then generalize to the Nth.
fields.Answer:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- general N: DENSE_RANK handles ties
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) ranked
WHERE rnk = :n;
  • The MAX-below-MAX form returns NULL automatically when there is only one distinct salary, because MAX over zero rows is NULL.
  • The window version returns zero rows when there is no Nth; wrap it as a scalar subquery SELECT (...) AS nth to get NULL.
  • DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER or RANK: with salaries 100, 100, 90 the second highest is 90. ROW_NUMBER gives 100; RANK skips to 3 for 90.

Alternative: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1, fine for small N.

Complexity: a sort or an index scan on salary; with an index on salary the LIMIT/OFFSET form reads only N distinct entries.

Pitfalls: forgetting the outer DISTINCT (tied rows return the same salary several times), NULL salaries (sorted first with DESC in Postgres unless NULLS LAST).
fields.Hint: DENSE_RANK so ties share a rank.
fields.Fact: Use DENSE_RANK for 'Nth highest distinct value'; ROW_NUMBER and RANK mishandle ties.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Window Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Aggregate Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html)

fields.Question: Given employees(id, name, salary, department_id), return the top 3 earners in each department, including ties at the boundary.
fields.Answer:
SELECT department_id, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT e.*,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id
                            ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC;
  • PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per department. You cannot filter on a window function in WHERE of the same SELECT, hence the subquery or CTE.
  • Ties: DENSE_RANK keeps everyone tied at the top three distinct salaries; ROW_NUMBER gives exactly 3 rows per department (state the tie-break you use).
  • For few departments with an index on (department_id, salary DESC), a LATERAL join with LIMIT 3 per department avoids sorting the whole table.
SELECT d.id, top.name, top.salary
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT name, salary FROM employees e
  WHERE e.department_id = d.id
  ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3
) top;

Complexity: window version is O(n log n) for the sort; LATERAL version is about 3 index probes per department.

Follow-up: clarify with the interviewer whether ties should be included; that decides ROW_NUMBER vs DENSE_RANK.
fields.Hint: Window function with PARTITION BY, filter in an outer query.
fields.Fact: Top-N per group is ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK partitioned by the group, filtered outside.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Window Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Table Expressions (joins, GROUP BY, LATERAL) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html)

fields.Question: Table events(user_id, event_type, created_at, payload). Return each user's most recent event. How do you make it fast on 500M rows?
fields.Answer:
-- portable
SELECT user_id, event_type, created_at
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                 ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM events e
) t
WHERE rn = 1;

-- PostgreSQL shortcut
SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) user_id, event_type, created_at
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC;
  • Index (user_id, created_at DESC) lets the database read groups in order.
  • Both forms still scan every row. When there are few users and many events per user, iterate users and take the first index entry each (LATERAL LIMIT 1, or a recursive CTE 'loose index scan').
  • At 500M rows the usual production answer is to maintain a user_latest_event table updated on write (upsert) rather than computing it at read time.

Pitfalls: GROUP BY user_id with MAX(created_at) then joining back returns duplicates when two events share the timestamp; add a unique tie-breaker (id) to ORDER BY.

Complexity: O(n log n) without the index, O(n) with it, O(users x log n) with the LATERAL trick.
fields.Hint: ROW_NUMBER = 1 or DISTINCT ON, backed by (user_id, created_at DESC).
fields.Fact: Greatest-n-per-group needs a deterministic tie-breaker and an index matching PARTITION BY plus ORDER BY.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: SELECT DISTINCT ON (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Window Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)

fields.Question: Table daily_revenue(day DATE, amount NUMERIC). Write a query showing each day's revenue, running total, and 7-day moving average.
fields.Answer:
SELECT day,
       amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running_total,
       AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day
                         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_revenue
ORDER BY day;
  • The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all peers with the same ORDER BY value. For unique days that is a running total; with duplicate keys peers get the same total, so use ROWS if you want strict row-by-row.
  • ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING counts rows, not days. If days can be missing, either fill gaps first (generate_series LEFT JOIN) or use RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (Postgres 11+).
  • The first 6 rows average fewer than 7 days; filter or flag them if the business needs full windows.

Complexity: one sort by day plus O(n) window evaluation.

Follow-ups: per-store running totals (PARTITION BY store_id), month-to-date (PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', day)).

fields.Fact: Moving averages over rows break when days are missing; fill gaps or use a RANGE interval frame.

fields.Question: Find customers who have never placed an order. Write it, and explain why NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) can return zero rows.
fields.Answer:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);

-- equivalent anti-join
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

The NOT IN trap: if any orders.customer_id is NULL, c.id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) evaluates to NULL (unknown) for every customer that is not 1 or 2, so no row passes. NOT EXISTS has no such problem.

  • Planners turn NOT EXISTS and the LEFT JOIN form into an anti-join; NOT IN often cannot be, because of NULL semantics.
  • Index orders(customer_id) makes each probe cheap.
  • In the LEFT JOIN form, test a NOT NULL column of orders (its PK), not a nullable one.

Complexity: hash anti-join O(customers + orders), or index nested loop O(customers x log orders).

Follow-up: 'customers with no orders in the last 30 days' goes inside the NOT EXISTS subquery, not in the outer WHERE.
fields.Hint: Anti-join: NOT EXISTS, never NOT IN with nullable columns.
fields.Fact: NOT IN against a subquery containing NULL returns nothing; use NOT EXISTS.

fields.Question: Table logins(user_id, login_date DATE) with possibly several logins per day. Find each user's longest streak of consecutive login days.
fields.Answer:
Pattern: gaps and islands. For consecutive dates, date - ROW_NUMBER() is constant within a streak, so it works as a group key.

WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         login_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                          ORDER BY login_date))::int AS grp
  FROM days
),
streaks AS (
  SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len,
         MIN(login_date) AS start_day, MAX(login_date) AS end_day
  FROM grouped
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
SELECT user_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY user_id;
  • DISTINCT first is essential: two logins on the same day would otherwise break the arithmetic.
  • Alternative: LAG(login_date) and start a new group when the gap is more than 1 day, then a running SUM of the 'new group' flags.

Complexity: one sort per user partition, O(n log n) overall.

Follow-ups: current streak (the island whose end_day is today or yesterday), timezone of 'day' (convert timestamps to the user's local date before casting).
fields.Hint: Gaps and islands: date minus ROW_NUMBER is constant per streak.
fields.Fact: Subtracting a row number from consecutive dates yields a constant that identifies each run.

fields.Question: A users table has duplicate emails (case-insensitive) due to a missing constraint. Write SQL to find them, delete all but the lowest id per email, and prevent it happening again.
fields.Answer:
-- find
SELECT lower(email), COUNT(*), array_agg(id ORDER BY id)
FROM users GROUP BY lower(email) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- delete all but the lowest id
DELETE FROM users u
USING users keep
WHERE lower(u.email) = lower(keep.email)
  AND u.id > keep.id;

-- prevent
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_lower_uniq
  ON users (lower(email));
  • Portable alternative: DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY id) rn FROM users) t WHERE rn > 1).
  • Before deleting, repoint or merge child rows (orders, sessions) to the kept id, or the FK will block or cascade unexpectedly. Do it in one transaction, in batches on a large table.
  • CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes, but fails (leaving an INVALID index) if duplicates sneak in during the build, so stop the source of duplicates first.

Pitfalls: deleting without a backup or dry-run count, the self-join form being O(n^2) per duplicate group if groups are large (the window version is safer).

Follow-up: application must handle the unique violation (23505) on signup gracefully.
fields.Hint: Self-join or ROW_NUMBER > 1, then a unique expression index.
fields.Fact: Fix duplicates by merging children, deleting rn > 1, then adding a unique index so they cannot return.

fields.Question: Table orders(id, created_at, amount). Write a query for monthly revenue and month-over-month growth percentage.
fields.Answer:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
  • Aggregate first, then window: window functions run after GROUP BY, so LAG sees one row per month.
  • NULLIF(prev, 0) avoids division by zero; the first month has NULL growth.
  • Months with no orders are missing, so LAG would compare to two months back. Generate the month series and LEFT JOIN if that matters.
  • Integer division: multiply by 100.0 (or cast) so you do not get truncated integers.

Follow-ups: year-over-year (LAG(revenue, 12) only if no months are missing), timezone of month boundaries (date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')).
fields.Hint: Aggregate in a CTE, then LAG over the result.
fields.Fact: Compute monthly totals first, then LAG; guard division by zero and missing months.

fields.Question: Tables users(id, signup_date) and activity(user_id, activity_date). Compute day-1 retention by signup cohort day: of users who signed up on day D, what fraction were active on day D+1?
fields.Answer:
SELECT u.signup_date AS cohort,
       COUNT(*) AS signups,
       COUNT(a.user_id) AS retained_d1,
       ROUND(COUNT(a.user_id)::numeric / COUNT(*), 3) AS d1_retention
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, activity_date FROM activity
) a
  ON a.user_id = u.id
 AND a.activity_date = u.signup_date + 1
GROUP BY u.signup_date
ORDER BY cohort;
  • LEFT JOIN keeps users who did not return; COUNT(a.user_id) counts only the matches, COUNT(*) counts all signups.
  • The D+1 condition lives in the ON clause. Putting it in WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join and retention becomes 100 percent.
  • DISTINCT on activity prevents a user with three events on D+1 being counted three times.

Generalize: for a retention matrix, join on activity_date - signup_date BETWEEN 0 AND 30 and group by cohort and day offset, then pivot with conditional aggregation.

Pitfalls: most recent cohorts have not had D+1 yet (exclude them), user timezones.

Index: activity(user_id, activity_date).
fields.Hint: LEFT JOIN with the condition in ON; COUNT(col) vs COUNT(*).
fields.Fact: Filters on the right side of a LEFT JOIN belong in ON, or you silently turn it into an inner join.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: A dashboard needs signups per day for the last 30 days, including days with zero signups. Table: users(id, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ).
fields.Answer:
SELECT d.day::date,
       COUNT(u.id) AS signups
FROM generate_series(
       date_trunc('day', now()) - INTERVAL '29 days',
       date_trunc('day', now()),
       INTERVAL '1 day') AS d(day)
LEFT JOIN users u
  ON u.created_at >= d.day
 AND u.created_at <  d.day + INTERVAL '1 day'
GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day;
  • Drive from a calendar (generate_series or a permanent dates table) and LEFT JOIN the facts onto it, so empty days appear with 0.
  • COUNT(u.id), not COUNT(*): COUNT(*) would count the calendar row and report 1 on empty days.
  • Half-open range join >= day AND < day + 1 uses an index on created_at; created_at::date = d.day wraps the column in a function and prevents index use.
  • Without generate_series (MySQL 8): a recursive CTE producing the dates, or a calendar table.

Follow-up: 'day' in which timezone? Use AT TIME ZONE on the series bounds for the business timezone.
fields.Hint: Calendar table LEFT JOIN facts, COUNT(fact_column).
fields.Fact: To show zero rows, generate the full date range and LEFT JOIN data onto it.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Table employees(id, name, salary, manager_id). List employees who earn more than their direct manager. Then: list each manager's full reporting chain depth.
fields.Answer:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- depth of each employee below the CEO
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT * FROM chain ORDER BY depth;
  • Self join: the same table under two aliases, one per role.
  • Inner join excludes the CEO (manager_id NULL), which is correct for this question.
  • Recursive CTE: anchor member (roots) UNION ALL recursive member joined to the previous level. Index manager_id.

Pitfalls: cycles from bad data make recursion infinite; guard with a depth limit or Postgres CYCLE clause (14+).

Follow-up: total salary cost under each manager (recursive CTE carrying the root id, then GROUP BY).
fields.Hint: Self join with two aliases; recursive CTE for hierarchies.
fields.Fact: Hierarchies in one table use self joins for one level and recursive CTEs for arbitrary depth.

fields.Question: Table orders(id, status, created_at) with statuses pending, paid, refunded. Produce one row per month with a column count per status and the refund rate.
fields.Answer:
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending')  AS pending,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded,
       ROUND(AVG((status = 'refunded')::int), 3)   AS refund_rate
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
  • Portable form: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). FILTER is standard SQL, supported by Postgres and SQLite, not MySQL.
  • One pass over the table, versus three separate subqueries or a self join per status.
  • AVG of a 0/1 expression is a rate, a neat trick worth mentioning.

Pitfall: dynamic column lists (unknown statuses) cannot be expressed in static SQL; return rows (month, status, count) and pivot in the application.

Complexity: O(n) scan plus the group aggregation.
fields.Hint: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) or SUM(CASE ...).
fields.Fact: Pivot with conditional aggregation in a single pass instead of joining one subquery per value.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Aggregate Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html)

fields.Question: Implement 'increment the page view count for (page_id, day)' so it is correct under 1,000 concurrent requests and creates the row if it does not exist.
fields.Answer:
CREATE TABLE page_views (
  page_id BIGINT, day DATE, views BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (page_id, day)
);

INSERT INTO page_views (page_id, day, views)
VALUES ($1, current_date, 1)
ON CONFLICT (page_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET views = page_views.views + EXCLUDED.views;
  • Atomic: the conflict check and update happen under the row lock, so no lost updates. MySQL equivalent: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE views = views + 1.
  • Wrong answers: SELECT then INSERT or UPDATE in app code (race: two inserts, one fails, or lost increments); UPDATE ... SET views = 5 computed in the app (lost updates).
  • Needs a unique constraint on the conflict target.

Hot row problem: a viral page means every request serializes on one row lock. Fix by sharding the counter ((page_id, day, bucket) with random bucket 0..15, SUM on read) or buffering counts in Redis/memory and flushing every few seconds.

Follow-up: exactly-once counting from a queue needs an idempotency key, not just an upsert.
fields.Hint: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET x = x + 1.
fields.Fact: Atomic upsert avoids races; split hot counters into buckets to avoid single-row contention.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: INSERT (ON CONFLICT) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Tables orders(id, customer_id) and order_items(order_id, product_id). Find customers who bought product 'A' but never bought product 'B'.
fields.Answer:
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id
HAVING BOOL_OR(oi.product_id = 'A')
   AND NOT BOOL_OR(oi.product_id = 'B');

-- portable
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN oi.product_id = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN oi.product_id = 'B' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0;
  • One grouped pass answers both conditions; alternatively EXISTS for A AND NOT EXISTS for B.
  • Common mistake: WHERE product_id = 'A' AND product_id <> 'B' filters rows, not customers, and returns everyone who bought A.
  • The set version: customers with A EXCEPT customers with B.

Complexity: O(n) aggregation over order items; restrict to product_id IN ('A','B') in WHERE first to shrink the input (then customers with neither are naturally excluded).

Follow-up: 'bought A and then later B' needs timestamps and a self join or MIN() per product compared.
fields.Hint: Group per customer, HAVING with conditional aggregates.
fields.Fact: Conditions about a set of rows per entity go in HAVING over a group, not in a row-level WHERE.
fields.Source:

PostgreSQL Documentation: Subquery Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html)

fields.Question: Write a query for the median and p95 response time per endpoint from requests(endpoint, duration_ms). Why is AVG often the wrong metric here?
fields.Answer:
SELECT endpoint,
       percentile_cont(0.5)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms) AS p50,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms) AS p95,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM requests
GROUP BY endpoint;
  • percentile_cont interpolates between values; percentile_disc returns an actual value from the set.
  • Latency is long-tailed, so the mean is dragged by outliers and hides what most users feel; p50 shows typical, p95/p99 shows the tail.
  • Exact percentiles need a sort per group, O(n log n) and memory heavy on billions of rows. At scale, use approximate sketches (t-digest, HDR histogram, approx_percentile in warehouses) or pre-aggregated histograms.
  • MySQL has no percentile_cont; emulate with ROW_NUMBER and COUNT over the partition, picking the middle rank.

Pitfall: averaging per-minute p95s to get an hourly p95 is mathematically wrong; percentiles do not compose, histograms do.
fields.Hint: Ordered-set aggregate percentile_cont WITHIN GROUP.
fields.Fact: Percentiles do not average; keep histograms or sketches if you need to roll them up.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Aggregate Functions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question:
This query takes 4 seconds on a 200M row table. What index do you add, and in what column order? Why?

SELECT id, total, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1 AND status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
fields.Answer:
Index: equality columns first, then the sort column, so the database seeks straight to the matching range already in the requested order and stops after 20 entries.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_cust_status_created
  ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at DESC);
  • Plan goes from scan plus sort of all matching rows to an index range scan with no sort node, reading about 20 index entries plus 20 heap fetches.
  • Order rule: equality predicates, then range or ORDER BY column. Putting created_at first would force scanning by time and filtering customers.
  • Leftmost prefix: this index also serves WHERE customer_id = ? alone, but not WHERE status = ? alone.
  • Add INCLUDE (total) or list the selected columns to get an index-only scan if the SELECT is narrow.

How to prove it: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after; look for the Sort node disappearing and rows read dropping.

Pitfalls: building the index without CONCURRENTLY on a live table (blocks writes), adding a separate index per column and hoping the planner combines them (bitmap AND cannot provide order for LIMIT).

Follow-ups: if status has many values queried via IN, the sort may come back; consider a partial index per hot status.
fields.Hint: Equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column.
fields.Fact: A composite index ordered equality-then-sort turns filter plus sort plus limit into a short range scan.
fields.Source:

Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
