fields.Question:
Both queries below are slow despite indexes on users(email) and orders(created_at). Explain why and rewrite them.

SELECT * FROM users  WHERE lower(email) = 'ada@example.com';
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-03-01';
fields.Answer:
Cause: wrapping the indexed column in a function or expression means the btree on the raw column cannot be used (the predicate is not sargable), so the planner scans.

-- 1: index the expression (and store emails normalized going forward)
CREATE INDEX users_lower_email ON users (lower(email));

-- 2: rewrite as a half-open range on the raw column
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-03-02';
  • Other non-sargable patterns: WHERE amount * 1.1 > 100, WHERE col + 0 = 5, WHERE COALESCE(col, 0) = 5, leading-wildcard LIKE '%x'.
  • Implicit casts: in MySQL comparing a VARCHAR column to a number (WHERE phone = 5551234) casts every row and skips the index. Pass a string.
  • Collations: ILIKE or case-insensitive comparisons may also skip a plain btree; use citext, an expression index, or a case-insensitive collation.

Verify: EXPLAIN shows Index Scan or Bitmap Index Scan instead of Seq Scan.

Rule of thumb: keep the column bare on one side of the comparison, move all computation to the constant side.
fields.Hint: Is the column wrapped in a function? Make the predicate sargable.
fields.Fact: Keep indexed columns bare in predicates or index the exact expression you filter on.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Indexes on Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-expressional.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

fields.Question: An admin page lists orders with ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET 200000 and page 4,000 takes 6 seconds. Why, and how do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Why: OFFSET does not skip for free; the database must produce and discard 200,000 rows before returning 50, so cost grows linearly with page depth. Rows inserted between page loads also shift pages, causing duplicates or skipped rows.

Fix: keyset (seek) pagination. Remember the last row's sort key and ask for rows after it, using a unique tie-breaker.

CREATE INDEX orders_created_id ON orders (created_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_created_at, $last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;
  • Every page is an index seek plus 50 entries: constant time regardless of depth.
  • Row-value comparison (a, b) < (x, y) works in Postgres and MySQL 8 and matches the composite index.
  • The cursor returned to the client is an opaque token encoding (created_at, id).

Tradeoffs: no 'jump to page 4,000' and no exact total page count. If the UI truly needs page numbers, cap the depth or use approximate counts.

Pitfall: sorting by a non-unique column without a tie-breaker skips or repeats rows at page boundaries.
fields.Hint: Seek past the last seen key instead of OFFSET.
fields.Fact: OFFSET costs O(offset); keyset pagination with a unique tie-breaker is O(page size) per page.
fields.Source:
Use The Index, Luke: Paging Through Results (https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)

fields.Question: A jobs table has 300M rows and a status column; 99.9% are 'done', and workers poll WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100. An index on status exists but the query is still slow and the index is huge. What do you do?
fields.Answer:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_pending_created
  ON jobs (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_status;
  • A partial index contains only the pending rows, so it is tiny, stays in memory, and is ordered by created_at, which also serves the ORDER BY LIMIT.
  • The query's WHERE must imply the index predicate (literal status = 'pending'); a parameterized status = $1 may not match with generic plans.
  • Low-cardinality full indexes are usually useless for common values and only help for the rare ones; the planner will seq scan for 'done' anyway.
  • MySQL has no partial indexes: use (status, created_at) composite, or move pending jobs to a separate small table.

Related: for a queue, combine this with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers do not block each other.

Pitfall: heavy churn (pending to done) makes dead index entries; autovacuum must keep up, or the small index bloats.
fields.Hint: Index only the rows you query: partial index.
fields.Fact: Partial indexes keep a hot, selective subset small and ordered, unlike an index on a skewed status column.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Partial Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: CREATE INDEX (CONCURRENTLY) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html)

fields.Question: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a nested loop where the planner estimated 10 rows from the outer side but actually got 2,000,000, and the query takes minutes. What is going on and how do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Diagnosis: a cardinality misestimate. Nested loop is great for 10 outer rows and terrible for 2M (2M inner index probes). The plan is wrong because the planner's statistics are wrong.

Fix in order:

  1. Run ANALYZE table (stats may be stale after a bulk load; autovacuum's analyze may not have run yet).
  2. Raise the statistics target for skewed columns: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET STATISTICS 1000; ANALYZE t;
  3. Correlated columns (city and zip): the planner multiplies selectivities assuming independence. Create extended statistics: CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies) ON city, zip FROM t;
  4. Check for expressions or functions the planner cannot estimate; expression indexes also gather stats on the expression.
  5. Rewrite as last resort: CTE MATERIALIZED, splitting the query, or temporarily SET enable_nestloop = off only to confirm the diagnosis.

How to read the plan: compare rows= estimated vs actual rows= node by node; the first node where they diverge by orders of magnitude is the root cause.

Pitfall: adding indexes blindly; the problem is the estimate, not missing access paths.
fields.Hint: Compare estimated vs actual rows per node.
fields.Fact: Bad plans usually come from bad row estimates; fix statistics before rewriting queries.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Using EXPLAIN (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Statistics Used by the Planner (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html)

fields.Question: A Python API endpoint listing 100 blog posts with their authors is slow. Logs show 101 queries per request. Explain the problem and fix it in code.
fields.Answer:
N+1 queries: one query for posts, then one query per post for its author. Each round trip has latency (often 1 ms or more), so 101 round trips dominate even if each query is fast.

# bad: one query per post
posts = db.fetch_all("SELECT id, title, author_id FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 100")
for p in posts:
    p["author"] = db.fetch_one("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = %s", (p["author_id"],))

# good: one batched query for all authors
posts = db.fetch_all("SELECT id, title, author_id FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 100")
ids = list({p["author_id"] for p in posts})
authors = {
    row["id"]: row
    for row in db.fetch_all("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ANY(%s)", (ids,))
}
for p in posts:
    p["author"] = authors.get(p["author_id"])
  • Or a single JOIN; batching (WHERE id IN / ANY) is better when the child side is one-to-many and would duplicate parent rows.
  • ORMs: SQLAlchemy selectinload / joinedload, Django select_related (FK, join) and prefetch_related (many, separate IN query).
  • Detect it with query counting in tests or APM traces.

Complexity: 2 round trips instead of N+1; same rows read.

Pitfall: huge IN lists (tens of thousands); chunk them or use a join against a temp table or VALUES list.
fields.Hint: Batch with WHERE id = ANY(list) or eager-load.
fields.Fact: N+1 is a round-trip problem; fetch related rows in one batched query.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Subquery Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html)

fields.Question: A reporting query SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 day' GROUP BY customer_id uses an index on created_at but still does millions of heap reads. How can you make it read only the index, and what can stop that working in PostgreSQL?
fields.Answer:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_created_cover
  ON orders (created_at) INCLUDE (customer_id, total);
  • A covering index contains every column the query touches, enabling an Index Only Scan: no heap fetch per row.
  • INCLUDE adds payload columns that are stored but not part of the search key (Postgres 11+, SQL Server). In MySQL InnoDB, put them in the key: (created_at, customer_id, total); secondary indexes already include the PK.
  • Postgres caveat: index-only scans still check the visibility map. Pages recently modified are not all-visible, so the heap is visited anyway. Keep autovacuum healthy (or VACUUM after bulk loads); EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Heap Fetches: N.

Tradeoffs: bigger index, slower writes, and every UPDATE to an included column must touch the index (and in Postgres disables HOT updates for that row).

Follow-up: for dashboards over large windows, pre-aggregate into a daily rollup table instead.
fields.Hint: Put every referenced column in the index; watch Heap Fetches.
fields.Fact: Covering indexes avoid table lookups; in Postgres they rely on the visibility map kept current by vacuum.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
MySQL Reference Manual: Clustered and Secondary Indexes (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-index-types.html)

fields.Question: A write-heavy events table (40k inserts per second) has 14 indexes added over time by different teams, and insert latency is climbing. How do you decide what to drop and what tradeoffs do you explain?
fields.Answer:
• Every index is maintained on every INSERT (and on UPDATEs to indexed columns): 14 indexes means roughly 15 btree writes, more WAL, more replication lag, more cache pressure.
  • Find unused ones: pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan = 0 over a long enough window (include month-end jobs; check replicas separately since stats are per server). MySQL: sys.schema_unused_indexes.
  • Find redundant ones: an index on (a) is redundant with (a, b) for most queries; duplicates with identical definitions happen often.
  • Keep: unique constraints and PK (they enforce correctness), FK-supporting indexes if you delete parents.

Process: drop with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY one at a time, watching query latency; in MySQL 8 first mark it INVISIBLE to test safely, then drop.

Structural options: move analytical queries to a replica or warehouse with their own indexes; partition by time so old partitions need no write-path indexes; consider BRIN on append-only timestamp columns (tiny, cheap to maintain).

Pitfall: deciding from one day of stats; rare but critical queries (billing runs) may be the only users of an index.
fields.Hint: Every index taxes every write; prove an index is unused before dropping.
fields.Fact: Indexes speed reads at the cost of every write; audit with usage stats and drop safely.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: CREATE INDEX (CONCURRENTLY) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Table Partitioning (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-partitioning.html)

fields.Question: Product wants search-as-you-type over 50M product names using WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $q || '%'. It seq scans. What are your options?
fields.Answer:
• A btree only helps prefix matches (LIKE 'abc%' with text_pattern_ops or C collation). A leading wildcard means any position, so btree is useless.
  • Trigram index (pg_trgm): GIN index on trigrams supports LIKE/ILIKE '%x%' and similarity search. Good up to a few tens of millions of rows; queries under 3 characters cannot use it well.
  • Full-text search (tsvector + GIN): word-based with stemming and ranking; does not do arbitrary substrings.
  • Dedicated search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Meilisearch): typo tolerance, relevance, facets. Cost: another system to keep in sync (CDC or outbox).
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY products_name_trgm
  ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

SELECT id, name FROM products
WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'
ORDER BY similarity(name, $1) DESC
LIMIT 10;

Answer shape: trigram GIN inside Postgres for a simple substring box, search engine once relevance, typos and facets matter.

Pitfalls: debounce on the client so you do not query per keystroke; GIN indexes slow writes (fastupdate pending list).
fields.Hint: Btree cannot do '%x%'; trigrams or a search engine can.
fields.Fact: Substring search needs trigram GIN or a search engine; btree only serves prefixes.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Full Text Search (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

fields.Question: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events on a 1B row PostgreSQL table takes 90 seconds and the dashboard calls it on every page load. Why is it slow, and what would you do?
fields.Answer:
• Postgres MVCC: different transactions can see different row counts, so there is no single stored count; it must scan (an index-only scan helps only if pages are all-visible). MySQL InnoDB has the same issue; only MyISAM kept an exact count.
  • Do you need exact? Usually not. Use the planner estimate: SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'events' (updated by VACUUM/ANALYZE), or EXPLAIN's row estimate for filtered counts.
  • Exact and fast: maintain a counter table updated by trigger or by the app in the same transaction. Beware: one counter row becomes a hot spot; use several bucket rows and SUM them.
  • Periodic: a materialized view or rollup table refreshed every minute; the dashboard reads that.

For filtered counts (WHERE tenant_id = ?), an index on tenant_id with a well-vacuumed table gives an index-only scan.

UI fix: show '10,000+' after counting up to a limit (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM events WHERE ... LIMIT 10001) t).
fields.Hint: MVCC means no stored exact count; estimate, cache or maintain counters.
fields.Fact: Exact COUNT(*) is a scan under MVCC; use estimates, rollups or bucketed counters.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Concurrency Control (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-intro.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Routine Vacuuming (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: This query is slow even though both columns have their own index: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1 OR phone = $2. What happens in the planner and how can you help it?
fields.Answer:
• A single btree index cannot answer an OR across two different columns. Postgres can use a BitmapOr of two bitmap index scans; MySQL has index_merge union. Often the planner (especially with a generic plan or bad estimates) just seq scans.
  • Rewrite as UNION so each branch uses its own index:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1
UNION
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = $2;
  • UNION (not UNION ALL) removes the duplicate when one user matches both.
  • OR on the same column is fine: status IN ('a','b') is a single index scan with multiple keys.
  • OR combined with ORDER BY LIMIT is harder; each UNION branch can do its own ORDER BY LIMIT, then sort the union.

Verify with EXPLAIN that you get two index scans or a BitmapOr, not Seq Scan.

Pitfall: OR with a nullable optional parameter (WHERE ($1 IS NULL OR email = $1)), the catch-all pattern, generates poor generic plans; build the SQL dynamically with only the filters present.
fields.Hint: One index per branch: rewrite OR as UNION.
fields.Fact: OR across columns often defeats indexes; UNION lets each branch use its own index.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Using EXPLAIN (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)
Use The Index, Luke: SQL Indexing and Tuning, Markus Winand (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

fields.Question: A query is 5 ms in staging and 30 seconds in production with the same schema and indexes. Walk through how you debug it.
fields.Answer:
1. Get the real plan in prod: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a replica, or auto_explain / pg_stat_statements / MySQL slow log to capture it from real traffic.
  2. Data distribution: prod has 1000x the rows and skew (one tenant with 40% of data). A plan that is fine for small tenants explodes for the whale.
  3. Statistics: stale or default stats targets in prod; check last analyze time.
  4. Parameterized and prepared statements: Postgres switches to a generic plan after 5 executions if it seems no worse; the generic plan may suit average values but not skewed ones. Compare with plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan.
  5. Cache state: staging data fits in RAM; prod reads from disk (BUFFERS shows read vs hit).
  6. Contention: the query is waiting, not working. Check pg_stat_activity wait_event and pg_locks for lock waits behind a long transaction or migration.
  7. Bloat: dead tuples from a disabled or lagging autovacuum make scans read far more pages.

Key insight: distinguish 'slow because it does more work' (plan, data, stats) from 'slow because it waits' (locks, IO, CPU saturation). The plan with actual timings tells you which.

Pitfall: tuning in staging with unrealistic data volumes.
fields.Hint: Is it working (plan, data) or waiting (locks, IO)?
fields.Fact: Production slowness is usually data skew, stats, generic plans, cold cache or lock waits; get the real plan.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Using EXPLAIN (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Statistics Used by the Planner (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Routine Vacuuming (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)

fields.Question: Two requests withdraw from the same wallet at the same time. The code reads the balance, checks it is enough, and writes balance = old - amount. Under READ COMMITTED, what goes wrong and give three ways to fix it.
fields.Answer:
Anomaly: lost update. Both read 100, both subtract 80 and write 20. The account paid out 160 from 100, and one write silently overwrote the other.

Fix 1: atomic conditional UPDATE (simplest and best when the logic fits in SQL):

UPDATE wallets
SET balance = balance - $amount
WHERE id = $id AND balance >= $amount
RETURNING balance;     -- 0 rows means insufficient funds

Fix 2: pessimistic lock: SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = $id FOR UPDATE, check in code, UPDATE, COMMIT. The second transaction blocks on the row until the first commits.

Fix 3: optimistic concurrency: read version, then UPDATE ... SET balance = $new, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $id AND version = $read_version; 0 rows updated means someone else won, so retry.

  • Also valid: REPEATABLE READ in Postgres (second writer gets a serialization error and retries) or SERIALIZABLE.
  • Add a ledger: insert an immutable transaction row in the same transaction; balance becomes a cached sum that can be audited.

Pitfalls: doing the check in application memory without a lock or guard; a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint is a good last line of defence.
fields.Hint: Read-modify-write race: make it atomic, lock it, or version it.
fields.Fact: Lost updates come from read-modify-write; use a guarded atomic UPDATE, FOR UPDATE, or a version check.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Explicit Locking (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Hospital rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call and both click 'go off call' at the same moment. Each transaction checks SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call is at least 2, then updates its own row. Both succeed and nobody is on call. Name the anomaly, explain why snapshot isolation allows it, and fix it.
fields.Answer:
Write skew. Each transaction read the same snapshot (count = 2), then wrote a *different* row. There is no write-write conflict, so snapshot isolation (Postgres REPEATABLE READ, Oracle SERIALIZABLE, MySQL REPEATABLE READ with plain reads) lets both commit. The invariant depends on rows neither one locked.

Fixes:

  • Run at true SERIALIZABLE (Postgres SSI detects the read-write dependency cycle and aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001; the app retries).
  • Lock the rows the decision depends on: SELECT ... FROM doctors WHERE on_call AND shift_id = $s FOR UPDATE before counting. The second transaction waits, then re-reads and sees count = 1.
  • Materialize the conflict: lock a single parent row (SELECT ... FROM shifts WHERE id = $s FOR UPDATE) that every such transaction must touch.

Same pattern elsewhere: double booking a meeting room, two users claiming the same username via check-then-insert, spending the same coupon twice.

Pitfall: FOR UPDATE cannot lock rows that do not exist yet (phantoms); for 'insert if none exists' use a unique constraint or a materialized lock row.

Follow-up: why does Postgres REPEATABLE READ prevent lost updates but not write skew? It detects concurrent updates to the same row, not dependencies through reads.
fields.Hint: Same snapshot, different rows written: SERIALIZABLE or lock what you read.
fields.Fact: Write skew passes snapshot isolation because the conflicting writes touch different rows.
fields.Source:
A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Two concurrent bank transfers: T1 moves money A to B, T2 moves money B to A. Each does UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = from then UPDATE ... WHERE id = to. Production logs show 'deadlock detected'. Explain and fix.
fields.Answer:
Cause: T1 locks A then waits for B; T2 locks B then waits for A. Cycle in the wait-for graph. The database detects it (Postgres after deadlock_timeout, default 1s; InnoDB immediately by default) and aborts one victim.

Fix: consistent lock ordering. Always lock accounts in a deterministic order, for example ascending id, regardless of transfer direction.

BEGIN;
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE id IN ($from, $to)
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $amt WHERE id = $from AND balance >= $amt;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $amt WHERE id = $to;
COMMIT;
  • Keep transactions short: no network calls or user waits while holding locks.
  • Still retry on deadlock (40P01 in Postgres, error 1213 in MySQL): deadlocks can also come from foreign key checks, triggers and index gap locks.
  • Batch updates should touch rows in a sorted order too (UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) does not guarantee order; lock with ORDER BY first).

Pitfall: treating deadlocks as fatal errors instead of retryable ones, or raising lock timeouts which only makes the stall longer.
fields.Hint: Lock in a global order (sort ids).
fields.Fact: Deadlocks are lock-order cycles; acquire locks in a consistent order and retry the victim.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Explicit Locking (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)
MySQL Reference Manual: Deadlocks in InnoDB (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-deadlocks.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Lock Management settings (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-locks.html)

fields.Question: You get paged: InnoDB deadlocks spiked after a deploy. How do you find which statements are involved and what are the usual root causes?
fields.Answer:
Gather evidence:

  • MySQL: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS shows the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK with both transactions, the statements, the locks held and waited for (index name, record vs gap lock). Turn on innodb_print_all_deadlocks to log every one.
  • Postgres: the server log has 'deadlock detected' with both PIDs and statements; set log_lock_waits = on to see waits above deadlock_timeout. Live: join pg_locks with pg_stat_activity.

Usual root causes:

  • Inconsistent lock order between two code paths (the new deploy probably added one).
  • Missing index: an UPDATE or DELETE with a WHERE on an unindexed column scans and locks many rows (InnoDB locks every row it examines under REPEATABLE READ).
  • InnoDB gap or next-key locks under REPEATABLE READ: two transactions insert into the same gap after both doing a locking read; switching that path to READ COMMITTED removes most gap locks.
  • Foreign keys: inserting a child takes a shared lock on the parent; concurrent parent updates conflict.
  • Long transactions holding locks while doing slow work.

Fix pattern: reproduce with two sessions, then order locks, add the missing index, shorten transactions, and make the code retry deadlock errors with backoff.

Good closing line: a low steady deadlock rate with retries is acceptable; a spike after a deploy is a code change to find.
fields.Hint: Read the deadlock report: which index, which lock type.
fields.Fact: Deadlock reports show both statements and lock types; common culprits are order, missing indexes and gap locks.
fields.Source:
MySQL Reference Manual: Deadlocks in InnoDB (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-deadlocks.html)
MySQL Reference Manual: InnoDB Locking (gap and next-key locks) (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-locking.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Lock Management settings (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-locks.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Explicit Locking (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)

fields.Question: Implement a job queue on PostgreSQL where 20 workers each grab the next pending job without two workers taking the same job and without them blocking each other.
fields.Answer:
-- claim one job
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'pending' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY run_at
  LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs j
SET status = 'running', locked_by = $worker, locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
FROM next
WHERE j.id = next.id
RETURNING j.*;
  • FOR UPDATE locks the chosen row; SKIP LOCKED makes other workers skip rows already locked instead of waiting, so they pick the next job.
  • Commit the claim right away and process outside the transaction, then mark done. Otherwise a long job holds a transaction open (blocks vacuum).
  • Crash recovery: a reaper resets jobs running with locked_at older than a timeout back to pending. That means jobs can run twice, so handlers must be idempotent (at-least-once delivery).
  • Index: partial index ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'pending'.

Wrong answers: SELECT then UPDATE without locking (two workers grab the same job); FOR UPDATE without SKIP LOCKED (workers queue behind each other).

When to move off Postgres: very high throughput or fan-out; use a broker (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ). Below a few thousand jobs per second, a table queue is simpler and transactional with your data.
fields.Hint: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, claim then commit.
fields.Fact: SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent workers claim different rows without blocking; handlers must still be idempotent.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: SELECT (including FOR UPDATE and SKIP LOCKED) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Partial Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)

fields.Question: Your service moves to SERIALIZABLE isolation. Write the Python transaction wrapper you would use, and explain which errors to retry.
fields.Answer:
import random, time
import psycopg
from psycopg import errors

RETRYABLE = (errors.SerializationFailure, errors.DeadlockDetected)

def run_in_tx(pool, work, max_attempts=5):
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        with pool.connection() as conn:
            conn.isolation_level = psycopg.IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE
            try:
                with conn.transaction():
                    return work(conn)
            except RETRYABLE:
                if attempt == max_attempts:
                    raise
        time.sleep(min(0.5, 0.01 * 2 ** attempt) * random.random())
  • Retry the whole transaction from the start, including the reads: the decision was based on data that changed. Never retry just the failed statement.
  • Retry SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure) and 40P01 (deadlock_detected). Do not retry constraint violations or syntax errors.
  • Exponential backoff with jitter avoids retry storms where the same transactions collide again.
  • work must have no side effects outside the database (emails, HTTP calls), or they would repeat; do them after commit or via an outbox.

Complexity: abort rate grows with contention; keep serializable transactions short and touch few rows.

Pitfall: read-only transactions can also fail under SSI; mark them READ ONLY (and DEFERRABLE for long reports) to reduce aborts.
fields.Hint: Retry the whole function on 40001 and 40P01 with jittered backoff.
fields.Fact: Serializable needs whole-transaction retries, and the work must be safe to repeat.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)

fields.Question: Mobile clients sometimes retry a 'charge card' request after a timeout, causing double charges. Design the database side of an idempotent payments API.
fields.Answer:
Idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it on every retry. The server stores it with a unique constraint and the outcome.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  request_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL,            -- started | completed
  response JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
  1. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING to claim the key. If it already exists and is completed, return the stored response. If started, return 409 or wait.
  2. Check request_hash so a reused key with a different body is rejected.
  3. Perform the charge, then store the response and mark completed. Local DB writes (ledger row, order status) go in the same transaction as the completion.
  4. The call to the payment provider is outside your DB transaction, so pass the same idempotency key to the provider too (Stripe supports this).

Recovery: a key stuck in 'started' after a crash is resolved by asking the provider for the charge's status with that key, not by blindly charging again.

Pitfalls: generating the key on the server (retries get a new one), expiring keys too soon, treating timeouts as failures.

Follow-ups: retention (delete after 24h to 7 days), exactly-once is really at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
fields.Hint: Client key plus unique constraint plus stored response.
fields.Fact: Idempotency keys turn at-least-once retries into a single effect, end to end including the provider.
fields.Source:
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, Stripe Engineering (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
PostgreSQL Documentation: INSERT (ON CONFLICT) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A flash sale has 100 units and 50,000 users click buy within a second. How do you prevent overselling, and how do you keep the database from melting?
fields.Answer:
Correctness: decrement with a guarded atomic update in the order transaction.

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE sku = $sku AND available > 0
RETURNING available;           -- no row: sold out

Only 100 transactions can succeed. A CHECK (available >= 0) constraint is a safety net.

Contention: every buyer serializes on one row lock, so throughput is limited to one commit at a time on that row. Options:

  • Split stock across N bucket rows (10 rows of 10) and pick a random non-empty bucket.
  • Gate in front of the DB: an atomic counter in Redis (DECR, or a Lua script) admits only the first 100 into the checkout path; the DB remains the source of truth.
  • Reservation with expiry: decrement creates a hold with expires_at; unpaid holds are released by a job. Prevents carts from locking stock forever.
  • Queue requests and process sequentially if latency can be relaxed.

Pitfalls: check available in a SELECT, then decrement in a separate statement (oversell under READ COMMITTED); hot-row lock waits piling up and exhausting the connection pool (set lock_timeout and fail fast).

Follow-up: reconcile Redis and the DB after the sale.
fields.Hint: Guarded UPDATE ... WHERE available > 0; shield the hot row.
fields.Fact: A conditional decrement prevents oversell; buckets, a cache gate, or a queue handle the contention.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Explicit Locking (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Client Connection Defaults (statement and lock timeouts) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: An analyst opened a transaction in a SQL client six hours ago and went to lunch. What problems can that cause in PostgreSQL, and how do you detect and prevent it?
fields.Answer:
• Vacuum cannot clean up dead rows newer than the oldest snapshot: tables and indexes bloat, queries slow down, and in the extreme you approach transaction ID wraparound.
  • Locks: even a SELECT holds an ACCESS SHARE lock; a later ALTER TABLE waits for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and every query behind it queues, causing an outage.
  • Replication: on a hot standby with hot_standby_feedback, the long query also holds back cleanup on the primary; without it, replicas cancel queries or lag.
  • Connections: an 'idle in transaction' session holds a connection slot.

Detect:

SELECT pid, usename, state, now() - xact_start AS age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY xact_start
LIMIT 10;

Prevent: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (for example 5 minutes), statement_timeout for app roles, analysts on a replica or warehouse, alerts on oldest transaction age. Terminate with pg_terminate_backend(pid) when needed.

MySQL equivalent: long transactions grow the InnoDB undo log (history list length) and slow everything.
fields.Hint: Old snapshot blocks vacuum; queued lock waits behind DDL.
fields.Fact: Long transactions block vacuum, queue DDL lock waits and hold connections; set idle-in-transaction timeouts.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Routine Vacuuming (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Client Connection Defaults (statement and lock timeouts) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Explicit Locking (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)

fields.Question: Two support agents open the same customer record in a web form, both edit different fields, and save. The second save silently overwrites the first agent's change. Design a fix that works across HTTP requests.
fields.Answer:
You cannot hold a database lock across two HTTP requests, so use optimistic concurrency control with a version column.

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- read: return version with the form
SELECT id, name, phone, version FROM customers WHERE id = $1;

-- save: only if nobody changed it since
UPDATE customers
SET name = $name, phone = $phone, version = version + 1
WHERE id = $id AND version = $version_from_form;
-- 0 rows updated: conflict, show a diff or reload
  • HTTP mapping: send the version as an ETag, require If-Match, return 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch.
  • Alternatives: only update the fields actually changed (reduces conflicts but loses invariants across fields); last-write-wins with an audit trail if conflicts do not matter.
  • Pessimistic 'checkout' locks (a locked_by column with expiry) are for long editing sessions where conflicts are expensive, like documents.

Tradeoff: optimistic is cheap when conflicts are rare; under heavy contention retries waste work and pessimistic locking wins.

Pitfall: using updated_at timestamps as the version (clock resolution, clock skew between app servers).
fields.Hint: Version column checked in the UPDATE WHERE clause.
fields.Fact: Optimistic locking compares a version on write, which works across stateless HTTP requests.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: A nightly report sums account balances while transfers keep running, and occasionally the total is off by exactly one transfer amount. The report runs several SELECTs under READ COMMITTED. Explain and fix.
fields.Answer:
Cause: under READ COMMITTED each statement takes a new snapshot. A transfer committing between the report's SELECT of account A and its SELECT of account B is half-visible: money appears to vanish or duplicate. This is read skew (non-repeatable reads across statements).

Fix: run the report as one consistent snapshot.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE region = 'eu';
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE region = 'us';
COMMIT;
  • Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: every statement sees the database as of the first query, without blocking writers (MVCC).
  • Or compute it in a single statement, which is always consistent within itself even at READ COMMITTED.
  • Long reports: run on a replica, or use SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE in Postgres to get a snapshot guaranteed not to see anomalies, at the cost of possibly waiting to start.
  • MySQL InnoDB default REPEATABLE READ also gives a consistent snapshot for plain SELECTs from the first read.

Pitfall: taking table locks to get consistency, blocking all transfers.
fields.Hint: Per-statement snapshot vs one snapshot for the transaction.
fields.Fact: READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per statement; multi-statement reports need REPEATABLE READ.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
MySQL Reference Manual: Transaction Isolation Levels (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Concurrency Control (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-intro.html)

fields.Question: Signup does SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE username = $1 and inserts if nothing is found. Under load two users end up with the same username. Fix it properly.
fields.Answer:
Cause: check-then-act race. Both SELECTs run before either INSERT commits, both see nothing. Row locks cannot help because the row does not exist yet (a phantom).

Fix: let a unique constraint decide, and handle the violation.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_username_lower ON users (lower(username));

INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;          -- no row returned: taken
  • Without ON CONFLICT: just INSERT and catch unique_violation (SQLSTATE 23505 / MySQL 1062) and map it to 'username taken'. The pre-check is still fine for UX feedback, never for correctness.
  • Case and Unicode: normalize (lowercase, NFKC) before storing, or 'Bob' and 'bob' both get through.
  • Reservations during a multi-step signup: insert a reservation row with expiry under the same unique key.

General rule: invariants about uniqueness or existence across rows belong in constraints, not in application checks.

Pitfall: raising isolation to REPEATABLE READ does not fix it; snapshot isolation does not detect two inserts of different new rows unless a constraint conflicts.
fields.Hint: Unique constraint plus handle 23505; the pre-check is only UX.
fields.Fact: Check-then-insert races; only a unique constraint guarantees uniqueness.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: INSERT (ON CONFLICT) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (including exclusion constraints) (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Indexes on Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-expressional.html)

fields.Question: You are designing the backend for (a) a payments ledger, (b) a product catalog with very different attributes per category, and (c) storing 2M IoT sensor writes per second. SQL or NoSQL for each, and why?
fields.Answer:
• (a) Payments ledger: relational (Postgres, MySQL). Needs multi-row ACID transactions (debit and credit together), constraints, and ad-hoc auditing queries. Correctness beats horizontal write scale; shard by account later if needed.
  • (b) Catalog: usually still relational with a JSONB attributes column (GIN indexed) for per-category fields, keeping price, stock and category as real columns. A document store (MongoDB) is reasonable if the catalog is read as whole documents and rarely joined. Mention the tradeoff, do not reflexively pick NoSQL for 'flexible schema'.
  • (c) IoT ingest: a wide-column or time-series store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, or TimescaleDB/ClickHouse for analytics). Writes are append-only, partitioned by (device_id, time bucket), queried by device and time range; LSM-tree storage handles very high write rates and scales out linearly.

How to frame it: start from access patterns, consistency needs and scale, not from the data model alone.

  • Relational: joins, ad-hoc queries, transactions, constraints; vertical scale first, sharding is manual work.
  • Key-value or wide-column: known access patterns, massive scale, partition-local operations; you design tables per query and give up joins and most cross-partition transactions.
  • Document: aggregate-oriented reads of a whole entity; weaker for many-to-many relationships.

Pitfall: choosing NoSQL 'for scale' at a size one Postgres instance handles comfortably.
fields.Hint: Access patterns, consistency, scale; in that order.
fields.Fact: Pick storage by access pattern and consistency needs; 'flexible schema' alone rarely justifies NoSQL.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: JSON Types (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)
Apache Cassandra Documentation: Data Modeling (https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/data-modeling/index.html)

fields.Question: You added read replicas. Now users sometimes update their profile, the page reloads, and they see the old value. Why, and what are the fixes?
fields.Answer:
Cause: asynchronous replication lag. The write went to the primary; the follow-up read hit a replica that had not applied it yet. You lost read-your-writes consistency.

Fixes:

  • Route reads of data the user just modified (or all of that user's reads for N seconds after a write) to the primary.
  • Track the primary's log position after the write (Postgres pg_current_wal_lsn(), MySQL GTID) in the session; read from a replica only when its replay position has caught up (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()), else use the primary.
  • Sticky sessions per user to one replica gives monotonic reads (no going back in time between requests), but not read-your-writes on its own.
  • Synchronous replication with synchronous_commit = remote_apply makes the commit wait until the standby has applied it, at the cost of write latency.

Related anomalies to mention: monotonic reads (two replicas at different lag), consistent prefix (seeing a reply before the question in partitioned systems).

Pitfall: treating replicas as consistent and using them for check-then-write logic; writes and their checks must hit the primary.

Monitoring: alert on replica lag in seconds and bytes; take lagging replicas out of the pool.
fields.Hint: Async lag: route recent writers to the primary or wait for the LSN.
fields.Fact: Async replicas break read-your-writes; route by recency or by replication position.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Synchronous Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html#SYNCHRONOUS-REPLICATION)

fields.Question: Your primary Postgres dies and you promote an async replica. Product asks: could we have lost committed transactions, and what are the options to avoid that? What are the risks of automatic failover?
fields.Answer:
• Async replication: yes. The primary acknowledges commit after its local WAL flush; any WAL not yet shipped is lost on promotion. Loss is bounded by replica lag (RPO greater than 0).
  • Synchronous replication (synchronous_standby_names, synchronous_commit = on): commit waits for a standby to flush WAL, so promotion of that standby loses nothing (RPO = 0). Cost: higher commit latency and, with one sync standby, writes stall if it goes down. Use quorum (ANY 1 (s1, s2)) to tolerate one standby failing.
  • Semi-sync (MySQL): similar idea, falls back to async on timeout, so RPO is not strictly zero.

Automatic failover risks:

  • Split brain: the old primary was only partitioned, not dead, and keeps accepting writes. Need fencing (STONITH, revoke its VIP or storage) and a consensus-based manager (Patroni with etcd, orchestrator with raft).
  • False positives from network blips cause unnecessary failovers; tune detection timeouts.
  • Clients holding connections to the old primary; use a proxy or DNS with short TTL and target_session_attrs=read-write.

Answer shape: state the RPO and RTO the business needs, then choose async (fast, small loss window), sync quorum (no loss, slower writes), and a fenced, consensus-driven failover.
fields.Hint: Async means a loss window; sync quorum plus fencing.
fields.Fact: Async failover can drop acknowledged commits; synchronous quorum replication trades latency for zero data loss.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Synchronous Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html#SYNCHRONOUS-REPLICATION)
PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Your multi-tenant SaaS has outgrown a single Postgres. You need to shard the events table (2TB, growing). How do you choose the shard key, and what goes wrong with bad choices?
fields.Answer:
Criteria for a shard key:

  • Most queries include it, so they route to one shard (avoid scatter-gather).
  • High cardinality and even distribution of data and load.
  • Things that must be transactional together share it (all of a tenant's rows co-located).
  • Stable: changing a row's shard key means moving it.

Here: tenant_id (hash of it). Every query is already tenant-scoped, joins between a tenant's tables stay local, and per-tenant transactions remain single-shard.

Bad choices:

  • created_at or auto-increment id with range sharding: all new writes hit the last shard (hot spot).
  • A low-cardinality key (country): a few huge shards, can never split further.
  • user_id when most queries are by organization: every org dashboard becomes a scatter-gather.

Handling whales: one tenant larger than a shard needs its own shard or a compound key (tenant_id, bucket) at the cost of cross-bucket queries for that tenant.

Mechanics: a directory or lookup service (tenant to shard) is more flexible than pure hash modulo, which forces mass data movement when shard count changes. Tools: Citus (distribution column), Vitess (vindex).

Pitfall: global unique constraints and global secondary indexes do not exist across shards for free.
fields.Hint: Shard on what every query filters by; avoid monotonic keys.
fields.Fact: A good shard key routes most queries to one shard and spreads load evenly; monotonic keys create hot shards.
fields.Source:
Vitess Documentation: Sharding (https://vitess.io/docs/reference/features/sharding/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You shard user data with shard = hash(user_id) % N. Going from 8 to 10 shards would move most of the data. How do you design sharding so that adding capacity moves little data?
fields.Answer:
Problem: with modulo N, changing N remaps roughly (1 - 1/new N) of keys, close to 90 percent going from 8 to 10.

Options:

  • Many fixed logical partitions: hash into, say, 4,096 virtual shards once, and map virtual shards to physical nodes with a table. Adding a node moves whole virtual shards; the hash function never changes. This is what Vitess keyspace ranges, Cassandra vnodes, Elasticsearch shards and DynamoDB partitions do in spirit.
  • Consistent hashing: nodes and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node only takes keys from its neighbour, about 1/N of the data. Virtual nodes smooth out uneven ranges.
  • Directory-based: explicit key to shard lookup; most flexible (can move one big tenant), but the directory must be highly available and cached.

Moving the data online: copy the partition to the new node (snapshot plus change stream), let it catch up, briefly block writes for that partition, flip the routing map, then delete the old copy.

Pitfalls: clients caching stale routing maps (version the map and redirect), moving while serving traffic without throttling.

Follow-up: jump consistent hash (Google) gives minimal movement with no ring state, but only supports adding shards at the end.
fields.Hint: Fixed many logical shards, move whole shards.
fields.Fact: Pre-split into many logical partitions or use consistent hashing so adding nodes moves about 1/N of data.
fields.Source:
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees, Karger et al., 1997 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
Vitess Documentation: Sharding (https://vitess.io/docs/reference/features/sharding/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: On DynamoDB (or Cassandra) one partition key, a celebrity's post_id, gets 50k reads and writes per second during a viral moment and requests are throttled, while the table as a whole is mostly idle. What do you do?
fields.Answer:
Why: throughput is limited per partition (DynamoDB: about 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per partition), so total table capacity does not help a single hot key.

Reads:

  • Cache in front (DAX, Redis, CDN). Hot keys are the best cache candidates.
  • Replicate the hot item under N keys (post#123#0..9) and read a random one.

Writes (likes counter):

  • Write sharding: spread writes over post#123#shard-k with random k in 0..N-1 and sum on read, or aggregate periodically.
  • Buffer and batch: accumulate increments in memory or a stream (Kinesis, Kafka) and apply one update per second.
  • Separate the hot counter from the item so the item itself stays readable.

Design lesson: choose partition keys with high cardinality and uniform access; a key that represents a single popular thing will always be hot, so plan sharding for it.

Pitfall: raising provisioned capacity on the table, which does nothing for a single partition beyond adaptive capacity limits.
fields.Hint: Per-partition limits: cache reads, shard writes with suffixes.
fields.Fact: A hot key is capped by one partition's limits; cache reads and spread writes across suffixed keys.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/best-practices.html)
Apache Cassandra Documentation: Data Modeling (https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/data-modeling/index.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: After saving an order in Postgres, the service publishes an OrderCreated event to Kafka. Sometimes the DB commit succeeds but the publish fails (or the reverse), and downstream services disagree. How do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Problem: dual writes to two systems are not atomic. No ordering of 'commit then publish' or 'publish then commit' survives a crash between them.

Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the order. A separate relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total) VALUES ($1, $2, $3);
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload)
VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), $1, 'OrderCreated', $4::jsonb);
COMMIT;
  • Relay options: poll SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or tail the WAL with CDC (Debezium outbox router), which avoids polling.
  • Delivery is at-least-once (relay can crash after publishing, before marking sent), so consumers must be idempotent: dedupe on event id.
  • Ordering: publish with the aggregate id as the Kafka key so events for one order stay ordered within a partition.

Alternatives: CDC directly on business tables (couples consumers to your schema), event sourcing (events are the source of truth).

Pitfall: 2PC/XA across DB and broker: rarely supported well, slow, and blocks on coordinator failure.
fields.Hint: Same transaction writes the event row; relay publishes.
fields.Fact: The outbox pattern makes state change and event atomic by writing both in one DB transaction.
fields.Source:
Pattern: Transactional outbox, Chris Richardson, microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Checkout touches three services, each with its own database: orders, payments and inventory. How do you keep them consistent without a distributed transaction?
fields.Answer:
Saga: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or command that triggers the next; on failure, run compensating transactions for the steps already done.

  1. Orders: create order PENDING.
  2. Inventory: reserve items (or fail: then cancel order).
  3. Payments: charge (or fail: release reservation, cancel order).
  4. Orders: mark CONFIRMED.
  • Orchestration: a central coordinator (or a workflow engine such as Temporal or Step Functions) drives the steps and compensations. Easier to reason about and monitor.
  • Choreography: services react to each other's events. Looser coupling, harder to see the whole flow.
  • Each step uses an outbox to publish reliably and is idempotent, because messages can be delivered more than once.
  • Compensation is a business operation (refund, release), not a rollback; some steps (sending an email) cannot be undone, so place them last.

Isolation tradeoff: sagas are not isolated. Other requests see intermediate states (order pending, stock reserved). Use semantic locks (status fields), and design the UI around pending states.

Why not 2PC: coordinator failure blocks participants holding locks, and most modern datastores and brokers do not support XA well.
fields.Hint: Local transactions plus compensations; orchestration vs choreography.
fields.Fact: Sagas replace distributed transactions with local steps and compensating actions, giving up isolation.
fields.Source:
Pattern: Saga, Chris Richardson, microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html)
Pattern: Transactional outbox, Chris Richardson, microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You put Redis in front of the users table using cache-aside. Occasionally a user sees stale data for hours after an update. Explain the race and how to design the caching to avoid it.
fields.Answer:
Cache-aside read: get from cache, on miss read DB and SET cache. Write: update DB, then DELETE the cache key (deleting is safer than setting).

The race: reader A misses, reads old value from DB; writer B updates DB and deletes the key; A then SETs the old value it read. The stale value now lives until TTL (or forever without one).

Mitigations:

  • Always set a TTL so staleness is bounded.
  • Delete after commit, not before (deleting before commit lets a reader repopulate with the old value).
  • Delayed double delete: delete again a short time after the write.
  • Versioned values: store the row version with the cached value and only SET if it is newer (Lua script compare-and-set).
  • Invalidate from CDC (Debezium reading the WAL) so every committed change triggers a delete, even from other writers.

Other cache failure modes to mention: thundering herd on a hot key expiry (single-flight lock or early probabilistic refresh), cache penetration on keys that do not exist (cache negative results briefly), cold cache after restart.

Answer shape: caches trade consistency for latency; state the acceptable staleness and design TTL plus invalidation around it.
fields.Hint: Stale SET after a concurrent delete; TTL plus versioned or CDC invalidation.
fields.Fact: Cache-aside has a read-populate race with writes; bound it with TTLs and version or CDC-driven invalidation.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
Redis Documentation: Sorted sets (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/)

fields.Question: Design storage for application metrics in Postgres: 500M rows per day, queries are mostly the last 24 hours per service, and data must be deleted after 30 days.
fields.Answer:
CREATE TABLE metrics (
  service_id INT NOT NULL,
  ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  value DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts);

CREATE TABLE metrics_2026_10_18 PARTITION OF metrics
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-18') TO ('2026-10-19');

CREATE INDEX ON metrics (service_id, ts);   -- created on each partition
  • Daily range partitions: queries with a ts filter only touch recent partitions (partition pruning), and recent partitions stay in memory.
  • Retention: DROP TABLE (or DETACH) of the oldest partition is instant and creates no dead rows, unlike DELETE WHERE ts < now() - 30 days, which bloats and needs vacuum.
  • Create future partitions ahead of time with a scheduler (pg_partman or cron); an insert with no matching partition fails unless you add a DEFAULT partition.
  • Dashboards over 30 days: rollup tables (1-minute, 1-hour aggregates) instead of scanning raw data.
  • Consider BRIN on ts for very large append-only partitions; much smaller than btree.

When to leave Postgres: heavy aggregations over billions of rows fit columnar stores (ClickHouse, TimescaleDB compression, BigQuery) far better.

Pitfall: too many partitions (thousands) slows planning; primary keys and unique constraints must include the partition key.
fields.Hint: Range partitions by time; drop partitions for retention.
fields.Fact: Time partitioning makes recent queries prune to few partitions and turns retention into dropping a table.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Table Partitioning (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-partitioning.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Model an order system in DynamoDB. Access patterns: get a customer's orders newest first, get an order with its line items, and find all orders in status SHIPPED for a warehouse. How do you design keys?
fields.Answer:
Start from access patterns, not entities. In DynamoDB you design keys so each pattern is a single Query on one partition key.

  • Customer orders: PK CUSTOMER#123, SK ORDER#2026-10-18T10:00:00#o789. Query with ScanIndexForward=false for newest first.
  • Order with items (single-table design): PK ORDER#o789, SK META for the order and ITEM#001, ITEM#002 for lines. One Query returns the whole aggregate.
  • Shipped orders by warehouse: a global secondary index with GSI1PK WAREHOUSE#7#STATUS#SHIPPED and GSI1SK = order date. Sparse: only set these attributes on orders in that state, so the index only holds relevant items.

Why: no joins and Scan is expensive, so co-locate what is read together under one partition key and sort key order.

  • GSIs are eventually consistent and cost extra write capacity per item.
  • Transactions (TransactWriteItems) exist but are limited (up to 100 items) and cost double.
  • Avoid low-cardinality GSI partition keys (STATUS#SHIPPED alone is a hot partition); prefix with warehouse or add a shard suffix.

Tradeoff to state: this is fast and scales, but new access patterns may require backfilling a new GSI or remodeling; relational is better when queries are unknown upfront.
fields.Hint: Design keys per access pattern; one Query per pattern.
fields.Fact: In DynamoDB you model keys from access patterns, co-locating items read together and using sparse GSIs.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/best-practices.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: In a Dynamo-style store with replication factor N = 3, you choose write quorum W and read quorum R. Which settings give you 'reads see the latest write', what does it cost, and is that a guarantee of linearizability?
fields.Answer:
• If R + W > N, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum in at least one replica, so a read contacts at least one node with the latest acknowledged write. Common: N=3, W=2, R=2.
  • W=3, R=1: fast reads, but any one replica down blocks writes. W=1, R=1: fastest and most available, but reads can be stale.
  • Read repair and anti-entropy (Merkle trees) bring lagging replicas up to date.

Not linearizable even with R + W > N:

  • Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff (writes accepted by nodes outside the home set) break the overlap.
  • Concurrent writes resolved by last-write-wins with clocks can drop writes.
  • A write that failed on some replicas is not rolled back on the ones where it succeeded, so later reads may or may not see it.
  • A read concurrent with a write may see the new value, and a later read the old one.

Cassandra mapping: consistency level QUORUM for both reads and writes gives R + W > N within a datacenter; LOCAL_QUORUM per DC for multi-region.

Answer shape: quorums tune the latency, availability and staleness tradeoff; for true linearizability (leader election, unique constraints) use a consensus system or lightweight transactions (Paxos).
fields.Hint: R + W > N for overlap; still not linearizable.
fields.Fact: Overlapping quorums reduce staleness but sloppy quorums and LWW mean they do not guarantee linearizability.
fields.Source:
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
Apache Cassandra Documentation: Data Modeling (https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/data-modeling/index.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You need to rename users.fullname to users.display_name on a live system with many app servers that deploy gradually. A plain ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN would break old servers. Describe the zero-downtime plan.
fields.Answer:
Expand and contract (parallel change): never make a change that the currently running code cannot handle.

  1. Expand: add display_name (nullable, no default rewrite). Fast metadata change.
  2. Dual write: deploy code that writes both columns and still reads the old one. (Or a trigger that copies fullname to display_name.)
  3. Backfill: copy old values in small batches: UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname WHERE id BETWEEN $a AND $b AND display_name IS NULL.
  4. Switch reads: deploy code that reads display_name (still writing both, so rollback is safe).
  5. Stop writing the old column: deploy code that only uses display_name.
  6. Contract: drop fullname once no running code (including old pods, cron jobs, analytics queries) references it.
  • Each step is independently deployable and reversible until the final drop.
  • Add NOT NULL at the end using a CHECK constraint NOT VALID then VALIDATE (see adding constraints), avoiding a long exclusive lock.
  • Alternative for read paths: a view exposing both names during the transition.

Pitfalls: ORMs that SELECT * and cache column lists, forgetting background workers and BI tools, dropping the column in the same release as the switch.

Same pattern: splitting a table, changing a column's type, moving data to a new service.
fields.Hint: Expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract.
fields.Fact: Zero-downtime schema changes go through expand and contract so every running version stays compatible.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL Documentation: ALTER TABLE (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)

fields.Question: On a 300M row Postgres table, which of these migrations are safe to run during business hours: (1) add a nullable column, (2) add a column with a constant DEFAULT, (3) add a column with DEFAULT now() or random(), (4) change a column from INT to BIGINT, (5) add NOT NULL to an existing column? And what protects you if a lock waits?
fields.Answer:
• (1) Safe: metadata-only.
  • (2) Safe on Postgres 11+: the constant default is stored in the catalog, no table rewrite. Before 11 it rewrote the whole table.
  • (3) Not safe: a volatile default must be computed per row, so the table is rewritten under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Add nullable, backfill in batches, then set the default for new rows.
  • (4) Not safe: rewrites the table and all its indexes under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Use a new column plus backfill plus swap, or an online tool.
  • (5) Scans the whole table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE to verify. Safer: ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT c (weaker lock), then on Postgres 12+ SET NOT NULL uses the validated check and skips the scan.

Lock queue danger: even a metadata-only ALTER needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE briefly. If a long query holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every new query queues behind the ALTER: an outage from a 'safe' migration.

SET lock_timeout = '3s';
SET statement_timeout = '15min';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_note TEXT;
-- on lock_timeout failure: retry later with backoff

Follow-up: MySQL 8 supports ALGORITHM=INSTANT for adding columns; other changes need gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change.
fields.Hint: Rewrite or not? And always set lock_timeout.
fields.Fact: Know which ALTERs rewrite the table, and always run DDL with a lock_timeout to avoid lock-queue outages.

fields.Question: Alert: the orders.id INT (32-bit) primary key is at 1.9 billion and will hit 2,147,483,647 in about three weeks. The table is 800GB and referenced by four other tables. What do you do?
fields.Answer:
Immediate triage: confirm the rate and the exact limit; check every FK column referencing it is also INT (they overflow at the same time).

Plan (online, Postgres):

  1. Add id_new BIGINT to orders (and order_id_new on referencing tables).
  2. Trigger or dual write so new rows populate the new columns.
  3. Backfill in batches, throttled by replica lag.
  4. Build a unique index CONCURRENTLY on id_new; build indexes for the new FK columns.
  5. In a short maintenance transaction with lock_timeout: swap the column names, set the sequence as owned by the new column, make the PK constraint use the new unique index (ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX), recreate FKs as NOT VALID then VALIDATE.
  6. Drop the old columns later.

MySQL: gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change build a shadow table with the new type and cut over.

Emergency buys time: if ids are not exposed and nothing relies on positivity, restart the sequence at -2,147,483,648 to use the negative range while the migration runs. Risky; mention it as a last resort.

Prevention: use BIGINT for every surrogate key from day one; monitor sequence headroom (last_value vs type max).

Pitfall: ALTER COLUMN TYPE BIGINT directly: hours of ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and a full rewrite of table and indexes.
fields.Hint: New BIGINT column, backfill, swap; never ALTER TYPE in place on a huge table.
fields.Fact: Migrating a nearly full INT key online means a shadow BIGINT column, backfill, and a fast swap.

fields.Question: Write a Python backfill that sets users.normalized_email = lower(trim(email)) for 200M rows without locking the table for long, overwhelming replicas, or starting over if it crashes.
fields.Answer:
import time

BATCH = 5_000

def backfill(conn, start_id=0, max_lag_s=5.0):
    conn.autocommit = True
    last_id = start_id
    while True:
        upper = conn.execute(
            "SELECT max(id) FROM (SELECT id FROM users WHERE id > %s ORDER BY id LIMIT %s) t",
            (last_id, BATCH),
        ).fetchone()[0]
        if upper is None:
            break
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE users SET normalized_email = lower(trim(email)) "
            "WHERE id > %s AND id <= %s "
            "AND normalized_email IS DISTINCT FROM lower(trim(email))",
            (last_id, upper),
        )
        last_id = upper
        save_checkpoint(last_id)
        while replica_lag_seconds() > max_lag_s:
            time.sleep(1)
  • Keyset batches by primary key: each batch is an index range, short transaction, few locks held briefly.
  • Autocommit makes each UPDATE its own short transaction. Idempotent: the IS DISTINCT FROM guard skips rows already done, so resuming from the saved checkpoint (or from 0) after a crash is safe.
  • Throttle on replica lag (and optionally DB CPU); sleep between batches if needed.
  • New writes must also populate the column (app change or trigger) before or during the backfill, or the backfill chases a moving target.

Pitfalls: a single UPDATE users SET ... (one huge transaction: long locks, massive WAL, replica lag, bloat, all-or-nothing rollback); OFFSET-based batches (each batch slower than the last).

Complexity: O(n) total work, O(batch) per transaction.
fields.Hint: Keyset batches, short transactions, idempotent guard, throttle on lag.
fields.Fact: Backfill in short keyset-paged transactions that are idempotent and throttled by replication lag.

fields.Question: You need to add a foreign key orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) and a NOT NULL check on a big live table. A plain ALTER would take a lock that blocks writes while it scans 500M rows. How do you do it online in PostgreSQL?
fields.Answer:
SET lock_timeout = '3s';

-- 1: index the referencing column first (needed for fast deletes on customers)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

-- 2: add constraints without checking existing rows (brief lock only)
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_nn CHECK (customer_id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;

-- 3: validate existing rows; takes a weaker lock that allows reads and writes
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_customer_nn;
  • NOT VALID constraints are enforced for new and updated rows immediately, so the problem cannot get worse while you validate.
  • VALIDATE takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on orders (and ROW SHARE on customers for the FK), so normal traffic continues.
  • Clean bad rows first; validation fails on the first orphan or NULL.

Why the index matters: without an index on orders.customer_id, every DELETE or key UPDATE on customers scans orders to check references.

Follow-up: on Postgres 12+, ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET NOT NULL after a validated CHECK skips the full scan; then drop the check.
fields.Hint: NOT VALID first, VALIDATE later.
fields.Fact: Add constraints as NOT VALID, then VALIDATE separately to avoid a long blocking scan.

fields.Question: Your MySQL 8 table has 1.5B rows and you must add a composite index and change a column type. How do you do it online, and how do tools like gh-ost work?
fields.Answer:
• First check native online DDL: ALTER TABLE ... ADD INDEX ..., ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE builds an index while allowing writes (brief metadata locks at start and end). Request the algorithm explicitly so MySQL errors instead of silently copying the table.
  • Column type changes usually need ALGORITHM=COPY, which blocks writes. Use an online schema change tool.
  • Replicas apply DDL serially: a 6-hour in-place ALTER on the primary means about 6 hours of replica lag.

gh-ost:

  1. Create a ghost table with the new schema.
  2. Copy rows from the original in small chunks.
  3. Read the binlog (as a fake replica) to apply concurrent changes to the ghost table. No triggers, so less load and it can be paused or throttled.
  4. Cut over with a brief lock: atomically rename original to old and ghost to original.

pt-online-schema-change is similar but uses triggers on the original table to capture changes (more write overhead, harder to pause).

Operational points: throttle on replica lag, run during low traffic, require enough disk for a full copy, test the cutover on a replica, and make sure no FK constraints complicate the swap (gh-ost does not support FKs).
fields.Hint: Native INPLACE if possible; otherwise shadow table plus binlog plus rename.
fields.Fact: Online schema change tools copy into a shadow table, replay changes, and swap with a brief rename.
fields.Source:
gh-ost: GitHub's online schema migration tool for MySQL (https://github.com/github/gh-ost)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017 (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: After scaling the API from 20 to 200 pods, Postgres starts refusing connections ('too many clients') and latency spikes. Each pod has a pool of 20 connections. What is going on and how do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Cause: 200 pods x 20 = 4,000 connections against max_connections of a few hundred. Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory; thousands of mostly idle connections waste memory and contention on internal locks. More connections than CPU cores also does not add throughput.

Fixes:

  • Put a pooler in front: PgBouncer (or RDS Proxy, Pgpool) in transaction pooling mode multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a small server pool (tens, roughly a few times CPU cores).
  • Shrink per-pod pools; size the total by what the database can usefully run concurrently, not by pod count.
  • Fix long-held connections: no network calls while holding a transaction; release connections promptly.
  • Read traffic to replicas, each with its own pool.

Transaction pooling caveats: session state does not persist across transactions: SET without LOCAL, advisory session locks, LISTEN, temporary tables, and (before PgBouncer 1.21) named server-side prepared statements break.

Diagnose: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state (many idle or idle in transaction?), pool wait time metrics in the app.

Pitfall: raising max_connections to 5,000, which trades the error for memory pressure and worse throughput.
fields.Hint: Pods x pool size vs max_connections; add PgBouncer.
fields.Fact: Use a transaction pooler and size total connections to the database's cores, not to the number of app pods.

fields.Question: Database CPU is pinned at 100% and the app is timing out. You have 10 minutes. What do you look at, in what order, and what are the likely causes?
fields.Answer:
1. What is running now: pg_stat_activity (state, wait_event, query, query_start). Many identical queries? Long-running ones? MySQL: SHOW PROCESSLIST / performance_schema.
  2. What costs the most overall: pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time; compare calls and mean time against yesterday. A query whose plan flipped or whose call count jumped 100x stands out.
  3. Recent changes: deploys (new query or missing index), migrations, a batch job, traffic spike, a cache that expired (stampede).
  4. Plan check: EXPLAIN the top offender; look for seq scans and nested loops on large row counts.
  5. Mitigate first: kill runaway queries (pg_cancel_backend), disable the feature flag or job, roll back the deploy, add the missing index CONCURRENTLY, scale reads to replicas.

Likely causes: new query without an index, plan regression after stats change, N+1 storm from a code change, cache stampede sending all reads to the DB, autovacuum on a huge table (usually IO rather than CPU), lock pileups (show as waiting, not CPU).

After: postmortem with the query, add query-level alerts, statement_timeout on app roles so one bad query cannot take the database down.

Answer shape: observe, find the top consumer, correlate with changes, mitigate, then fix the root cause.
fields.Hint: pg_stat_activity now, pg_stat_statements overall, correlate with changes.
fields.Fact: For a hot database: find the top query, correlate with the latest change, mitigate fast, then fix.

fields.Question: A developer ran DELETE FROM orders without a WHERE at 14:32 in production. Walk through how you recover, and what backup setup makes this possible.
fields.Answer:
Stop the bleeding: do not restart or fail over. Note the exact time (or transaction id) of the bad statement from logs.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR): restore the latest base backup to a new server, then replay WAL (Postgres) or binlog (MySQL) up to just before the delete:

-- postgresql.conf on the restore server (Postgres 12+)
restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-18 14:31:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
-- then: touch recovery.signal and start the server
  1. Verify the restored data on the side server.
  2. Copy only the affected rows back into production (INSERT ... SELECT via postgres_fdw or a dump of the orders table), reconciling any rows created after 14:32.
  3. Promote the restore only if the whole database must roll back, which loses everything after 14:32.

Setup that makes this possible: regular base backups (pgBackRest, Barman, managed snapshots) plus continuous WAL archiving, retention covering your recovery window, and regularly tested restores. Replicas are not backups: the DELETE replicated to them instantly. A delayed replica (recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h') is a fast alternative for this exact scenario.

Prevention: least-privilege production access, require transactions in manual sessions, safe-update modes (MySQL --safe-updates).

Metrics to state: RPO (how much data loss is acceptable) and RTO (how long recovery may take).
fields.Hint: Base backup plus WAL replay to a target time on a side server.
fields.Fact: PITR replays archived WAL to just before the mistake; replicas are not backups.

fields.Question: You must move a 3TB Postgres database from self-hosted to a managed service (or to a new major version) with less than a minute of write downtime. Outline the plan.
fields.Answer:
1. Initial copy plus change stream: logical replication (publication on the source, subscription on the target) copies the tables and then streams ongoing changes. Alternatives: AWS DMS, pglogical, or physical replication if the target allows it.
  2. Prepare the target: schema created first (logical replication does not replicate DDL), extensions, roles, and indexes (or build them after the copy for speed).
  3. Verify: row counts and checksums per table, replication lag near zero, run read traffic or shadow queries against the target.
  4. Freeze DDL on the source for the duration.
  5. Cutover: stop writes (put the app in read-only or pause the writers), wait for lag to reach zero, advance sequences on the target (logical replication does not copy sequence values), switch the connection string or DNS, resume writes.
  6. Rollback plan: reverse replication from the new target to the old one, so you can switch back without losing new writes.

Pitfalls: tables without a primary key cannot replicate UPDATE and DELETE without REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; large objects are not replicated; forgetting sequences causes duplicate key errors right after cutover.

Key insight: downtime equals the time to drain lag and flip connections, so rehearse the cutover end to end on a copy.
fields.Hint: Logical replication, verify, short write freeze, sync sequences, switch.
fields.Fact: Migrate with a continuous change stream so downtime is only the final drain and switch; remember sequences.
